title: Greenland deal: What did the US and Denmark actually agree to?
text:
Greenland deal: What did the US and Denmark actually agree to?
The United States, Denmark, and Greenland finally came to terms on a deal that all sides are calling a victory toward their ends.
Over the weekend, the United States, Denmark, and Greenland announced an agreement that, at first blush, didn’t seem to agree at all.
President Donald Trump has long coveted Greenland for its strategic location and mineral wealth, even threatening to invade. The new deal, he said in a social media post, “gives the United States permanent control over security and all other needs in Greenland.”
Denmark and Greenland touted the deal as similarly historic, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it recognizes “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom [of Denmark] and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.”
President Donald Trump’s preoccupation with Greenland has been riling up Denmark, the rest of Europe, and Greenlanders. Many hope the adoption of the pact, which largely maintains the status quo, will finally put tensions to bed.
Details should emerge this week as both sides prepare to sign the deal at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. But it appears the agreement is an updated version of a pact signed between Greenland and NATO in 1951, which gives the United States new assurances and clearance for an expanded role.
For example, while the Greenlandic government remains in control of its own affairs, the deal “guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” such as minerals, a U.S. State Department official said according to Euractiv.
With Greenland inching toward independence, the agreement also appears to ensure the provisions will remain in force even if the island leaves its role as a semiautonomous territory in the kingdom of Denmark.
As a part of the arrangement, the United States is expected to open two new bases in Greenland. It currently operates Pituffik Space Base in the far north of the island. The U.S. had as many as 17 bases on Greenland during the Cold War.
The hope in Denmark and Greenland is that the agreement will mark the end of a tumultuous year in which Denmark faced the prospect of fighting the U.S. to defend the island.
“There is a big sigh of relief because this seems to be over,” says Jørgen Ullerup, a longtime reporter for Denmark’s Jyllands-Posten newspaper and author of “Harpoon Warriors,” a novel about a future invasion of Greenland.
The episode has brought Denmark and Greenland closer together despite a fraught colonial past. But it has left a negative mark on Danish-American relations.
“The Danish people have been among the most pro-American people in Europe,” says Mr. Ullerup. “Now, we’re among the most anti-American.”
